The Spurs’ winning streak is at eight games, over which they’ve ranked in the top three on both ends of the floor. They’re 8-2 for the second straight season, though they have a better point differential than they had through 10 games last year.

Two takeaways

  • Victor Wembanyama scored 52 points (adding 24 rebounds and eight blocks) against the Mavs on Wednesday … with a broken jump shot. After that game, he was 7-for-29 (24%) from mid-range and 12-for-50 (24%) from beyond the arc. But he scored 45 of those 52 points in the restricted area (13-for-16) or at the free throw line (19-for-23), and he may have found his shooting stroke over the weekend. He wasn’t as dominant inside, but made seven of his 12 3-point attempts in Sacramento and Portland.
  • The Spurs’ starting lineup still doesn’t play a ton of minutes; at 10.5 minutes per game, it ranks 13th among lineups that have played at least five games together. It was also outscored by the Kings on Friday. But it’s allowed just 85.8 points per 100 possessions, the best mark among the 22 lineups that have played at least 50 total minutes, and it’s been much better offensively (114.9 scored per 100) than the Spurs were when De’Aaron Fox, Dylan Harper and Stephon Castle shared the floor last season.

Coming up: The Spurs had the league’s best interconference record last season, going 26-4 in regular-season games (that counted in the standings) against the East. Their first interconference game this season is Wednesday in Chicago, the end of a four-game trip.

Despite the injuries, the Thunder are one of five teams with only two losses. And they’re looking dominant again, having beaten the Grizzlies and Wizards by a total of 70 points over the weekend.

Two takeaways

  • Over the course of 27 hours, the Thunder climbed from 12th to third on defense. The Grizzlies’ 97 points on 104 possessions on Friday was their worst offensive game of the season, and the Wizards’ 75 on 99 was the worst offensive game for any team by a wide margin. The two teams combined to shoot just 32-for-76 (42%) in the paint.
  • The Thunder have seen the league’s biggest drop, by a wide margin, in 3-point rate. They’ve taken just 35.5% of their shots from beyond the arc, the league’s second-lowest rate, down from 42.6% (13th highest) last season. But they’ve outscored their opponents in the paint in each of their last nine games. Ajay Mitchell’s 15.6 points in the paint per 36 minutes trail only the marks of Giannis Antetokounmpo and Victor Wembanyama among 287 players who’ve played at least 100 minutes total.

Coming up: The Thunder’s longest road trip of the season is only four games long, and it begins with a Tuesday-Wednesday back-to-back in Portland. They blew a 22-point lead and suffered their first loss of the season at the Moda Center around this time last year.

The Wolves lost two of their first three games without Anthony Edwards, but they’ve since won four straight. They handed the Rockets their first home loss (and worst defensive game) of the season on Wednesday and then ended the Pelicans’ four-game winning streak two nights later.

Two takeaways

  • All three of the Wolves’ losses came on their first stretch of five games in seven days, with two of them being rest-disadvantage games on the road. The other one (vs. Golden State) doesn’t look as bad now that the Warriors have won seven straight games as it did at the time, and the three losses have come by a total of just 17 points.
  • The starting lineup with Ayo Dosunmu in place of Edwards hasn’t been great offensively, even though Dosunmu has averaged a team-high 21.6 points, with 50/40/90 shooting splits, over the star’s seven-game absence. He’s one of seven players who’ve shot better than 50% on at least 25 catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts.

Coming up: The Wolves’ win over Utah on Sunday was the start of an eight-game homestand (tied for the longest in the league this season). They have a league-low five rest-advantage games this year, with the first of the five being a visit from the Bulls on Saturday.

Week 4: vs. DAL, vs. CHI

After a West-best 7-1 start, the Rockets have lost two straight games to slide out of the top four in the conference. They still have a league-high six wins over teams that enter Week 4 with winning records. (No other team has more than four.)

Two takeaways

  • The Rockets had a fourth-quarter lead against the Wolves and erased all of a 19-point deficit in Phoenix. But they scored just nine points on 12 clutch possessions (with Kevin Durant shooting 1-for-6) over the two games. Their three losses have come by a total of 18 points, while their seven wins have come by an average of 15.4.
  • Durant is the most efficient high-volume scorer (25-plus points per game) in NBA history, and his true shooting percentage of 64.9% would be his highest mark in the last four seasons. But his usage rate (23.1%) is the lowest of his career and he took just six shots from the field in the Rockets’ win over Boston last Monday. The other three returning starters have also seen (smaller) drops in usage, with Fred VanVleet and Marcus Smart both carrying more of a load than their ’25-26 counterparts.

Coming up: The Rockets have outscored their opponents 11.4 points per 100 possessions at home, and they’re back at the Toyota Center for three more games this week. The homestand begins with a marquee matchup with the Nuggets on Monday.

Week 4: vs. DEN, vs. GSW, vs. UTA*, @ WAS

The Sixers suffered their first loss with Joel Embiid in the lineup on Friday, unable to make another comeback from a huge deficit against the Cavs. But they got a big win in Detroit (avenging their previous loss) earlier in the week and remain at the top of the Eastern Conference.

Two takeaways

  • The Sixers already have as many clutch wins (eight) as the Nets had all of last season. The flip side of that is that, while they’re tied with the Lakers for the league’s best record, they have the 15th-best point differential (plus-3.1 per game), that of a team that’s 7-4. They’ve now scored 79 points on 57 clutch offensive possessions (139 per 100), getting contributions from almost everybody who’s seen the floor with the score within five points in the last five minutes.
  • The non-clutch offense hasn’t been so great, with the Sixers in the bottom five in the league in both effective field goal percentage and offensive rebounding percentage. They had two efficient games last week, but they were both against the Bulls’ 30th-ranked defense, and they’ve scored just 107.1 points per 100 possessions over their other nine.

Coming up: Jaylen Brown won’t make his return to Boston until Jan. 21, but he’ll face his former team for the first time on Tuesday. That’s the start of what could be a big, three-game homestand, especially if Tyrese Haliburton is back in the Pacers’ lineup by Sunday afternoon.

The Celtics lost in Houston (without Paul George) last week, but they’ll be playing for first place in the Eastern Conference on Tuesday. Having won their last two games by a total of 59 points, they’re in the top five on both ends of the floor for what would be the fifth straight season.

Two takeaways

  • The Celtics have been switching up their starting lineup. Neemias Queta has replaced Mitchell Robinson as the starting center (though they’ve also played a few minutes together), while Jordan Walsh, Baylor Scheierman, Hugo González and Mike Conley have all taken turns in the starting backcourt. Payton Pritchard remains a reserve, while Sam Hauser only started the game (Wednesday vs. Milwaukee) that Jayson Tatum missed. But Pritchard has played the fourth-most minutes on the team, and the Celtics have been at their best (plus-21.2 per 100 possessions) with Hauser on the floor.
  • The Celtics shoot a lot of 3s, but their opponents shoot more. Boston opponents have taken 51.2% of their shots from 3-point range, which would be the highest opponent rate in the 48 years of the 3-point line by a wide margin. Only 47% of their opponents’ 3-point attempts (the league’s eighth lowest rate) have been wide open, but they’re probably getting a little lucky, with opponents shooting just 32.7% (second lowest) on those wide-open 3s.

Coming up: There are just six teams with winning records in the Eastern Conference, and the Celtics’ first games against two of the six will be a road back-to-back on Tuesday and Wednesday. First up is a visit to Jaylen Brown and the Sixers, with first place in the East on the line.

Record: 5-4

OffRtg: 114.1 (15) DefRtg: 108.3 (7) NetRtg: +5.8 (9)

After a 0-3 start, the Knicks have won five of their last six games to climb over .500 for the first time. They’re one of two teams (the Rockets are the other) that haven’t lost a game that wasn’t within five points in the last five minutes, and last week’s three wins all came by double digits.

Two takeaways

  • OG Anunoby and Mikal Bridges are both still shooting below 30% from 3-point range, while Jalen Brunson is just 28-for-71 (39.4%) in the paint. But the offense has picked up (119.6 points scored per 100 possessions) over the 5-1 stretch. The shooting has been a little better, but they’ve also cut down on turnovers and continued to give themselves a ton of second chances.
  • The regular starting lineup has still scored less than a point per possession in its 95 total minutes. But last Monday, the Knicks turned their game against Brooklyn around with a 16-2 run with both Brunson and Bridges off the floor to start the fourth quarter. And with Josh Hart (ankle) out the last two games, the new starting lineup (with Landry Shamet) outscored the Bulls and Cavs by 16 points in its 23 minutes.

Coming up: The Knicks had a rest advantage when they won in Cleveland over the weekend, but they’ll be at a disadvantage when the two teams meet again at Madison Square Garden on Wednesday. Then they’ll head out of a four-game trip that includes their first two meetings with the Raptors. The Knicks won all five meetings last season by at least 16 points.

The Lakers have won five straight games and have the best record in the Western Conference. They’re also 2-0 without Luka Dončić, having held on after blowing almost all of a 26-point lead against the Pistons on Sunday.

Two takeaways

  • Dončić’s usage rate (39.8%) has dipped below the play-by-play era record of 40.2% (Russell Westbrook in 2016-17), but his efficiency remains high, and he had 18 free throw attempts as he recorded his second 50-point game of the season against Portland on Friday. His 40.1 points per game would be the third-highest mark in NBA history, and his true shooting percentage of 67.9% would be the highest for a player who averaged at least 32 (37 total instances).
  • The Lakers have a bottom-10 defense, even though they’re one of five teams that rank in the top 10 in both opponent field goal percentage in the paint (55.1%, seventh lowest) and the percentage of their opponents’ shots that have come in the paint (46%, ninth lowest). Only the Heat have allowed more 3-pointers per game, and no team has allowed more second-chance points per game.

Coming up: The Lakers’ win in Detroit on Sunday was the start of a four-game trip, and they’ll be at a rest disadvantage in Atlanta on Monday night. But after that, their next six games are against teams with a cumulative record of 10-48 (.172).

The Pistons dominated the Hornets (x 2) and Nets on a three-game winning streak, but couldn’t handle a step up in competition, falling to the Sixers and Lakers (without Luka Dončić) last week. They also announced Sunday that Jalen Duren (who’s been out since the first half of Game 2) won’t be back for at least another two weeks.

Two takeaways

  • The Pistons have been the league’s best second-half team, outscoring their opponents by 16.5 points per 100 possessions after halftime. But they’ve been outscored by 0.9 per 100 (19th) in first halves, and they couldn’t recover from a 37-14 Sixers run spanning the first and second quarters on Wednesday or a 38-14 first quarter from the Lakers over the weekend. They’ve trailed by double digits in six of their nine games, having done so in only 29 (35%) of their 82 last season.
  • The much bigger difference between the first-half Pistons and the second-half Pistons has been on offense. Duncan Robinson and Ausar Thompson have combined for an effective field goal percentage of 45.8% before halftime and 71.2% after, and the Pistons have also turned the ball over far less often in the second half.

Coming up: The Pistons don’t have any road trips longer than four games this season, and their first of four four-game trips begins in Washington on Thursday. The road team will have a rest advantage in both games against the Wizards this week.

Stephen Curry is on a heater and the Warriors have won seven straight games, even though they’ve trailed four of them by double digits. They ranked 29th defensively over their 0-3 start, but are sixth on that end of the floor over the course of the winning streak.

Two takeaways

  • Curry has averaged 33.8 points on a true shooting percentage of 73.3% over the streak, and he had 17 of the Warriors’ 29 clutch points in their overtime win over Orlando on Saturday. His season-long true shooting percentage of 70.8% would be the highest in NBA history for a player who averaged at least 30 points, topping his own mark of 66.9% in 2015-16.
  • Yaxel Lendeborg would have the highest true shooting percentage (63.0%) in NBA history for a rookie who averaged at least 20 points. He’s only 7-for-30 (23%) on pull-up 3-pointers, but he hit a huge one in overtime on Saturday. The Warriors had shot 1-for-13 on clutch shots over their first three games that were within five points in the last five minutes, but were 10-for-15 against the Magic.

Coming up: The Warriors won both of their games in San Antonio (a two-game series) last season, with Curry totaling 95 points on 57% shooting and 23-for-24 from the line. They’ll be back at the Frost Bank Center on Friday, with first place in West Group C (both teams are 1-0 in Cup play) on the line.

- Tyler Herro had a knee scare in the third quarter of another loss to the Celtics on Sunday, but he returned to the game. The Bucks have been one of the healthiest teams in the league, with their top nine guys in minutes per game having played in all 10 games. They’ve been outscored by just 1.9 points per 100 possessions in 143 minutes with their four full-time starters all on the floor, but have been outscored by 18.0 per 100 in 337 minutes with at least one of the four on the bench.
- Brayden Burries replaced Ryan Rollins in the starting lineup last week and has averaged 13.0 points in 28.6 minutes in his four games as a starter, up from 8.8 in 15.9 in his six games off the bench. He’s only 6-4, but he’s had much more success in the paint (63% shooting) and in getting to the free throw line (42 attempts per 100 shots from the field) than he’s had from the outside (8-for-36 from 3-point range).
Coming up: The Bucks’ last six games have come against teams that rank in the top 10 offensively, and they’ll be at a rest disadvantage when they host the Lakers’ top-ranked offense on Wednesday. Luka Dončić scored 41 points in a Lakers’ win in Milwaukee last November.
